name: Supramarginal gyrus, posterior division
summary: The posterior supramarginal gyrus lies between the anterior division and the angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule, above the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus. It is multimodal association cortex that integrates the location of the body and of objects around it and, in the dominant hemisphere, links the sounds of words to their spelling and to the movements of writing; in the right hemisphere it contributes to spatial attention and to the perception of one's own body. It is supplied by parietal branches of the middle cerebral artery, is a watershed with the posterior cerebral artery below, and its lesions add agraphia, spatial disorientation and elements of the Gerstmann syndrome to those of the anterior division.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule between the anterior supramarginal gyrus in front and the angular gyrus behind, above the superior temporal sulcus and below the intraparietal sulcus.

afferents.from: Superior parietal lobule and intraparietal cortex

function: This cortex represents the position of the limbs and of objects in body-centered coordinates for reaching and grasping, and links auditory word forms with their written form, supporting spelling and writing in the left hemisphere; it is part of the dorsal attention and the sensorimotor integration networks that keep the body schema updated. In the right hemisphere it participates in the sense of ownership of the limbs and in the perception of the contralateral hemispace, and its damage contributes to neglect, asomatognosia and anosognosia. It also receives vestibular input through the parieto-insular vestibular cortex, so lesions can produce a sensation of tilt or of leaving the body.

bestView.label: posterior supramarginal gyrus in front of the angular gyrus
inferior parietal lobule above the superior temporal sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: The middle part of the inferior parietal lobule on axial images above the atrium, between the upturned Sylvian fissure and the upturned superior temporal sulcus that marks the angular gyrus.

pathology.finding: Cortical restricted diffusion of the posterior inferior parietal lobule with agraphia and finger agnosia (left) or spatial neglect (right).
Bilateral inferior parietal and occipital atrophy with agraphia, acalculia and visuospatial disorientation.
Somatosensory auras of tingling, a feeling of the limb being absent or displaced, or vertigo, with a parietal EEG focus.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Disconnection of phonological and orthographic word forms in the dominant inferior parietal lobule
Loss of the right inferior parietal representation of contralateral space and body

lesionEffects.deficit: Disturbed body schema and vestibular illusions
lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the parietal vestibular and body-schema cortex

examination: Writing to dictation and spelling aloud
Line bisection, figure copying and drawing a clock
Ask about out-of-body sensations, tilt or the feeling that a limb is not theirs
pearls: Agraphia without aphasia is inferior parietal; test writing separately from speech
Asomatognosia (denial of one's own arm) is a right posterior parietal sign
Vertigo with a normal vestibular examination can be a parietal seizure

pitfalls: Anosognosia means the patient will not report the deficit; rely on examination and the family
